summary: Two topics: First, the agreed-upon ruling that when a replacement sin-offering is designated and then the original reappears, the original is left to die - it is still consecrated but has no remaining purpose. Second, R. Yehuda's teaching that the lottery is the essential designating act for the Yom Kippur goats: without the lottery, even a valid goat cannot serve as the Yom Kippur offering. The lottery is not mere selection but divine determination of which animal serves.

display.hint: If a designated sin-offering is lost, a replacement is brought. If the original then reappears, the original must be left to die - it cannot serve since the replacement already fulfilled its purpose.
display.title: The Stranded Original: When Replacement Seals the Outcome

learning.ahaMoment: Once a replacement is designated, the original sin-offering is in limbo: too holy to be released back into ordinary use, but no longer needed for its original purpose. It must die because it has no other legitimate use.
learning.memoryAnchor: Two animals, one role: when the replacement fills the purpose, the original is left in sacred limbo until it dies.
learning.learnerQuestion: If a Yom Kippur sin-offering was lost, replaced, and then the original reappears, what happens to each animal?
learning.coreTension: The original animal is still consecrated and technically valid - yet its ritual purpose has been fulfilled by the replacement. Can it serve another role, or is it permanently stranded?
learning.coreMove: The Gemara rules the original is left to die. The replacement already fulfilled the Yom Kippur purpose, so the original cannot serve as a sin-offering again. Yet it remains consecrated and cannot be sold. It is a holy animal with no remaining outlet.

takeaway.text: A consecrated animal whose designated purpose was fulfilled by a replacement is left to die - it cannot serve (purpose gone) and cannot be sold (still sacred).

learning.learningBlocker: Students assume that because the original is still valid and holy it must have some use. The key is the irreversibility of the purpose transfer: once the replacement fulfilled the specific Yom Kippur role, the original's sacred role is permanently vacated.

display.whats: R. Yehuda: the lottery designates the Yom Kippur goats; it is the act that makes them the Yom Kippur offering
display.hint: R. Yehuda teaches that the lottery is the essential designating act for the Yom Kippur goats - not just a procedure but the very act that transforms a valid goat into the Yom Kippur offering. Without the lottery, no goat can serve as the Yom Kippur offering.
display.title: The Lottery as Divine Designation, Not Random Selection

learning.ahaMoment: The lottery is not a randomizer but a divine designator. What appears as a chance mechanism reveals divine choice: God determines which animal becomes the Yom Kippur offering by determining the lot's outcome.
learning.memoryAnchor: The lottery as divine determination: what looks random reveals which goat God chose for His service.
learning.learnerQuestion: Why must the lottery always be performed for the Yom Kippur goats, even when both are identical and either could serve?
learning.coreTension: If both goats are identical and interchangeable, the lottery seems pointless. Yet R. Yehuda insists it is indispensable. Is the lottery a legal formality or something more essential?
learning.coreMove: R. Yehuda holds the lottery is not a selection mechanism but a designating act. Without the lottery, no goat acquires the status of 'Yom Kippur offering.' The lottery is divine designation that creates the halachic role - however valid the animal, without the lottery it has no status.

takeaway.text: The lottery is not mere randomization - it is the essential act that designates which goat serves God and which serves Azazel. Without it, neither goat has its Yom Kippur status.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may see the lottery as logistical selection and assume that when both animals qualify, it could be skipped. R. Yehuda teaches that the lottery is constitutive - it does not reveal which goat to use; it creates the goat's legal identity.

rashiTranslations.en: 'But according to Rav' - who says that the Mishnah teaches 'it shall graze' regarding the second of the second pair, and atonement is achieved through the first,
the rejected one - why? If this were like an individual's counterpart dying, this is not even a question for the Rabbis, who hold it does not die, since
atonement was achieved through the rejected one, and they say that one set aside to cover a loss is not treated like a lost animal. But even
according to Rabbi, it should not die here, for this one was not set aside to replace a lost animal, since originally
the first one still existed, and it was on account of the goat to be sent away that died
that he needed to bring two more; and since living
animals are not rejected from the start, he could have offered
either one, so it is as though he had set aside two sin-offerings
to cover a contingency, such that if one of them is lost, he offers
the other. 'And Rabbi Oshaya said' - the second
one shall graze, even according to Rabbi, since it was not set aside
to cover a loss. 'Since' - there is a mitzvah preference for the first
from the outset, when we set aside this second one,
we set it aside with the loss in mind, and it is no different
from one who sets aside an animal to cover a loss; and the Mishnah follows Rabbi's view, and so
we say in tractate Temurah that Rav
establishes the Mishnah in accordance with Rabbi. 'We learned: Rabbi Yehuda
says it shall die' - one might initially think that this refers to the very case where
the Rabbis say it shall graze, and Rabbi Yehuda says it shall die,
and this forces the conclusion that according to Rabbi Yehuda living
animals can become rejected, as is taught: if the blood is spilled, the one to be sent away
shall die. 'This works out well according to Rabbi Yochanan, who says'
the Mishnah's ruling applies to the second of the first pair - we learned it shall graze, and
Rabbi Yehuda says regarding it that it shall die, meaning atonement is achieved through the second of
the second pair. 'But according to Rav' - who says that it shall graze
was taught in the Mishnah regarding the second of the second pair, and it is regarding this one
that Rabbi Yehuda says it shall die. 'Through what is atonement achieved' -
for according to Rabbi Yehuda, atonement cannot be achieved through the first,
since he holds that living animals can become rejected. 'Do you think,' etc.,
'that it refers to the second of the first pair' - and he disputes on two points,
as I explained above. 'And some raise the challenge' -
this way: this first challenge that I raised
above, from 'and Rabbi Yehuda further said,' etc.,
which I raised above against Rav - some instead raise
it originally against Rabbi Yochanan, and this is how
they raise it: 'This works out well according to Rav' - who says that according to the first Tanna
living animals are not rejected, and regarding the second of the second pair
he says it shall graze, and Rabbi Yehuda does not say regarding that one
that it shall die; this is why he then says 'and furthermore,'
to teach that he holds living animals
can become rejected, and the 'it shall die' he says in the opening clause does not
refer to the very one the Rabbis say shall graze,
and he comes to disagree on two points: in the opening clause he disagrees
regarding a communal sin-offering, where the Rabbis say it shall graze
and Rabbi Yehuda says it shall die; and in the latter clause
he disagrees regarding living animals, where the Rabbis say they are not
rejected and atonement is achieved through the first, and he comes
to say that this one shall die and the second shall be offered. 'But
according to Rabbi Yochanan, what does "and furthermore" add' - for the Rabbis too
say the first becomes rejected? 'It is difficult' - as we said,
that the Mishnah is precisely in accordance with Rav. 'This works out well:
if the blood is spilled, the one to be sent away shall die, since
its mitzvah was not yet performed' - for the blood and the indispensable decree are written regarding the acts
performed in white garments, and he must bring other blood, and this is impossible without
a new lottery; and since he holds that living animals can become rejected, the first goat to be sent away shall die. 'But
if the one to be sent away dies' - why do you require a replacement, forcing him to bring two more and cast lots
and pour out the first blood? Its mitzvah has already been performed, for the goat to be sent away, the only thing
indispensable about it is the lottery alone, to establish which lot falls 'for the Name' upon its counterpart; for
we hear from Rabbi Yehuda himself that even if the confession was not said, it is still valid, and all the more so the sending itself is not
indispensable according to all opinions, since when 'the indispensable decree' is written, it is written regarding the acts the priest himself performs in white garments,
and not regarding acts performed by the designated man. 'To remain alive' - meaning it must not die before
the time of its counterpart's blood being placed; for if it dies before that, the atonement of the blood accomplishes nothing.
Therefore a replacement is needed, and this is impossible without a new lottery, requiring two more animals, and the original
is rejected, for all agree that among slaughtered animals, rejection applies. 'The townspeople who sent' - through a messenger,
their shekels to Jerusalem, to the Temple. 'If the terumah was already separated' - the three baskets, before it became known
that they were lost. 'They must take an oath' - the messengers take the oath of bailees to the treasurers, since the loss
falls on the Temple treasury, for the owners are not obligated to contribute the shekel again, as we learned (Ketubot 108a):
they separate the terumah on behalf of what was lost but not yet known. 'But if not' - if the terumah had not yet been separated,
the loss does not fall on the Temple treasury but on the owners; therefore they take an oath to the townspeople. 'They were found' -
referring back to 'were lost.' 'The thieves returned them' - referring back to 'were stolen.' 'And they are not credited to them' -

to the owners, and they must contribute the shekel again for the coming year. 'Obligations of this year' - meaning shekels set aside as an obligation for this year. 'The goats for idol worship' - when the community sins in idol worship by a court ruling,

they bring a bull for a burnt-offering and a goat for a sin-offering. 'And he set aside others in their place' - and the original ones were then found. 'All of them shall die' - and we do not say they may be offered in the coming year.
'Offerings' - the comment is completed on 65b as 'communal,' continuing to explain the communal-offering funding source discussed here.
